publicTrace: Base rate / reference class: The post-ARP-expansion SPM child poverty series (2022–2024) has averaged 13.2 pct, with the most recent published print at 13.4 pct (CY2024). Year-over-year changes in this regime have been small (−0.3 pct in the latest year), giving a tight empirical anchor.

Point estimate mechanism: A weighted blend of the PolicyEngine current-law microsimulation prior (13.0 pct, weight 0.55), the post-expansion Census SPM history (13.2 pct, weight 0.35), and the latest published value (13.4 pct, weight 0.10) yields a raw blend of ~13.1 pct; a macro adjustment of −0.05 pct for modest real-income growth and EITC/SNAP indexation produces a calibrated point estimate of 13.0 pct.

Uncertainty construction: The 80% CI is set at ±1.1 pct (lower) and ±1.3 pct (upper) around the point estimate, reflecting ASEC sampling variance (~0.3–0.5 pct), SPM expense/resource volatility (medical out-of-pocket, housing cost index), and policy uncertainty. The distribution is right-skewed because upside risks (benefit cliffs, immigration enforcement reducing take-up, SNAP/Medicaid cuts) are larger than downside risks.

Disconfirming consideration (outcome below interval): If real wages continue to outpace inflation and SNAP/Medicaid enrollment remains high, the rate could fall below 11.9 pct—outside the 80% interval—particularly if housing cost growth moderates and EITC refunds are larger than modeled.

Disconfirming consideration (outcome above interval): If federal benefit reductions (e.g., SNAP cuts, Medicaid unwinding, or CTC non-refundability changes) take effect in 2025, or if immigration enforcement substantially reduces transfer take-up among mixed-status families, the rate could exceed 14.3 pct.

Data availability caveat: The PolicyEngine input is a stored current-law prior (API v0.654.1), not a fresh server-side microsimulation for CY2025; the Census SPM tables page was reachable but no machine-readable 2025 data exists yet. Uncertainty is widened accordingly.

Calibration note: The CDF is asymmetric—the left tail is compressed (floor near 9.5 pct reflecting the post-ARP structural floor) and the right tail is extended to 17.5 pct to capture tail risks from large policy changes or economic shocks.
assumptions: PolicyEngine current-law prior of 13.0 pct is treated as a credible microsimulation anchor for CY2025 under no major legislative change, weighted at 0.55.
Post-ARP-expansion SPM child poverty history (2022–2024 average ~13.2 pct) is the primary empirical reference class, weighted at 0.35.
No major new federal child poverty legislation (e.g., expanded CTC) is enacted and fully effective for CY2025 income.
SNAP, Medicaid, and EITC remain at current-law parameters throughout 2025 without large mid-year administrative disruptions.
ASEC sampling and SPM methodology remain consistent with prior years; no major methodological revision is assumed.
dataCaveats: Census SPM tables page was reachable but contains no CY2025 data; the 13.4 pct anchor is the CY2024 published value used as a prototype seed, not a confirmed 2025 figure.
PolicyEngine input is a stored API prior (v0.654.1), not a fresh server-side microsimulation run for this specific forecast cell; uncertainty is widened to reflect this.

SPM includes medical out-of-pocket expenses and geographic housing cost adjustments that can move the series independently of income or transfer policy changes, adding volatility not captured in the point estimate.
Immigration enforcement actions in 2025 could reduce transfer program take-up among mixed-status families in ways not fully modeled by PolicyEngine current-law inputs.
SNAP and Medicaid administrative changes (unwinding, eligibility redeterminations) in 2025 may affect resource counts in ways that diverge from the historical reference class.
drivers: PolicyEngine current-law microsimulation prior anchoring near 13 pct
Post-ARP SPM child poverty historical mean (~13.2 pct, 2022–2024)
SNAP and Medicaid enrollment levels and any administrative disruptions
Real wage growth relative to SPM poverty thresholds (which include housing cost geography)
Federal tax credit refundability and EITC parameters for tax year 2025
